did_you_know.text: Did you know? The psalm opens with the heading “For the director of music. A psalm of David,” identifying it as a psalm of David and assigning it to the director of music.
Did you know? Two requests for protection appear at the very beginning of the psalm: “Rescue me” and “Guard me”—asking for deliverance and protection from an evil person and a violent man.
Did you know? The wicked are described as people who constantly plot evil in their hearts and “stir up wars”—creating conflicts and quarrels.
Did you know? The tongues of the wicked are compared to snakes, and the verse uses the image of venom under their lips to describe the danger of their words.
Did you know? The threat in the psalm is not merely verbal: the wicked set traps, spread nets, and place snares in order to “make” the worshiper’s steps falter.
Did you know? At the center of the psalm, the worshiper addresses the Lord directly: “You are my God,” and asks Him to listen to the voice of his pleas.
Did you know? The Lord is described as “the strength of my salvation” and as the one who shields the worshiper’s head on the day of battle—that is, in a time of conflict or war.
Did you know? The worshiper asks not only to be saved himself, but also that the Lord not allow the wicked to achieve their desires or let their schemes succeed.
Did you know? The psalm asks that the evil spoken by the wicked—“the trouble of their lips”—cover them and fall back upon them, as part of a prayer to thwart their way.

Did you know? Near the end of the psalm, a declaration of trust appears: the Lord will uphold justice for the poor and defend the cause of the needy. As a result, the righteous will give thanks to His name, and the upright will dwell in His presence.
